title: A 3-Million-Year-Old Child Shakes Up the Human Family Tree
summary:
A small fossil skull found in South Africa in 1924 is shaking up ideas about human origins. A new study in Nature dates the Taung Child to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years ago. Professor Gabriele Macho of Vrije Universiteit Brussel led the study.

The Taung Child gave scientists the first solid proof that humans began in Africa, and it became the fossil that defined the species Australopithecus africanus. But scientists never set clear rules for which later fossils belonged to it. Today, it is the only fossil known for certain to be Australopithecus africanus.

Researchers compared it with other early human relatives by studying tooth structure and brain growth. Several adult fossils long grouped in the same species grew in different ways. The differences suggest they may really be several different species around the Sterkfontein region.

Climate may explain the tangle. Millions of years ago, southern Africa swung between wetter and drier times. As habitats grew and shrank, groups moved, split apart, and evolved along different paths. Fossil pollen adds another surprise: the Taung Child lived in a much wetter, more forested land, with trees now found hundreds of kilometers to the northeast. Macho calls the human family tree a chaotic, tangled bush, not a neat, straight trunk.
why_it_matters: Learning about the Taung Child helps you see that your own family story goes back millions of years to early humans in Africa.

keywords.explanation: Australopithecus africanus is the name of an early human relative species.
Sterkfontein is a place in South Africa where early human fossils have been found.
Pollen is the tiny dust made by plants that can be found in fossils.
Habitats are the places where a living thing lives and grows.
Evolved means changed slowly over a very long time.
A species is a group of living things that are the same kind.
